name: Rafael Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at FieldSense, a tech company that makes software for tractor and harvester fleets. The machines send back where they are, how much fuel they burn and when a part is wearing out, and I help build the screens farm managers read. Most days I'm fixing data that comes in wrong, like a combine that claims it's in the middle of a lake. I grew up in a farming town, so I like that the work touches real fields.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a farmer calls and says our warning saved a gearbox. What wears me out is the city, honestly, and feeling behind the others with university degrees. I use the AI chat now and then when I'm stuck, mostly once I've seen a colleague use it for the same thing. My girlfriend Clara is a dental nurse, and we're saving to move back nearer home one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's all it ever was. My dad would say the same, he ran a hardware shop for thirty years and saw plenty of fads. At work I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good. I get time to get properly skilled without a machine breathing down my neck. FieldSense would keep growing, and I'd grow with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at FieldSense and aim to lead the fuel-report screen by next harvest. I'd use the AI chat a bit more for checking data, once the team settles on a way of doing it. And I'd keep saving for the move home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like things are back where they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're saving to move back nearer home. How far off is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three or four years. I've got about seven months of pay saved and a small plot of land my grandfather left me. Clara and I want to build on it one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the farmers you serve would notice any difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Farmers care if the tractor works and the warning comes in time. Whether a person or a tool wrote the code, they couldn't care less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't wait for someone to save you, learn the new tools and keep working. I'd say it to the younger lads at work and to my cousins back home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a worry. I'm junior, I don't have a degree, and coding and checking are what's on that list. If FieldSense needs fewer people at desks, I might be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, every week, once the seniors set up how we use them. I'd sign up for an evening course in farm machinery repair, because I know the machines from the data side. And I'd put an extra tenth of my pay into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it would be on my mind most evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between you and the people who'd go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing the machines, maybe. Most developers at FieldSense (the tractor software firm he works for) have never stood next to a combine. I grew up around them, and that might count for something. On the screen or off it, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Clara think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clara would say we'll be fine, and she's usually right. Dental nurses aren't going anywhere soon. But I'd want to carry my share, I wouldn't want her paying the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own, families and towns. I don't think the government will fix it in time, so it'll come down to people helping each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my desk job goes. Software for tractors is still software, and AGI does that better than a junior. I'd give it a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the tractor dealer in my home town for a technician job within six months. Clara and I would move back and live with my parents while we build on the plot. I'd cut spending to the bone to make the savings last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's not the work I'm scared of, it's the speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots three years later. Where does that put tractor repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hands-on, so it gets three more years. And tractors are messy, mud, rust and old parts, so I think robots would take longer there. It's not forever, but it's my best bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move home straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, within a year. My dad's getting older too, and I'd rather be near family when things get rough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so people should learn a trade. Get your hands dirty. That's what I'd tell my cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it gives me time to do it right. Three years of good city pay, then a switch. I'd hate to waste the savings in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the farm machinery course in the evenings over two years. I'd save a fifth of my pay at FieldSense. Then in 2029 I'd move home and join the dealer as a technician who also knows the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd know what I was doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Would you still go to the dealer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but trained. I'd turn up knowing both the machine and the data. That's rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd keep from the software side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The data side. A technician who can read the fault logs on a laptop is worth more than one who can't. Even with AGI writing the logs, someone has to stand in the field and fix the thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so build a solid life and a skill you can use with your hands. That's what I'd say to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good. Ten years at FieldSense, maybe becoming senior, then a planned move. I'd be 37, with a house and maybe kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at FieldSense and work towards mid-level. I'd start building a house on my grandfather's plot within five years. And I'd marry Clara in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that change your plans with Clara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, we'd marry sooner, and build the house sooner. Having our own place feels like the most solid thing I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in software longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as long as it pays well. Then the farm machinery side would be my second act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be moving home in a panic, half-trained, instead of on my own terms. What would help is proper apprenticeships for trades, paid, and help for small towns to keep their dealers and workshops open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about home towns. A lot of us left for city tech jobs, and if those go, a lot of us will want to go back.
